en: *The Path of Peace and Bliss for Wandering Minds*, composed by Master Wonhyo.

Regarding the wandering of the mind toward peace and bliss, seven gates are briefly opened: First, an exposition on the origin and fundamental intent of the teaching; Second, the determination of that...
First, the location of the land;
second, the clarification of doubts and hardships; third, the elucidation of the causes and conditions for rebirth;
and fourth, the manifestation of the factors for rebirth.
Five, enumerating the categories of those who attain rebirth;
six, discussing the ease or difficulty of rebirth;
seven, raising doubts and then resolving them.
Regarding the statement on describing the origin and essential tenets of the teaching:
Now, the nature of the minds of sentient beings is pervasive and unimpeded, as vast as empty space and as profound as the great ocean.
Because it is like empty space, its essence is equal and no distinct characteristics can be apprehended; how, then, could there be places of purity or defilement?
Because it is like the great ocean, its nature is moist and supple, able to follow conditions without resistance; how could there not be times of motion and stillness?
Thus, some may, due to the wind of defilements, revolve for a long time within the five turbidities, sinking into the waves of suffering and flowing on endlessly;
while others, relying on the power of goodness, cut off the four currents and do not return, reaching the other shore in eternal tranquility.
If this is so, both movement and stillness are but a great dream;

speaking from the perspective of awakening, there is neither "this" nor "that. Impure lands and pure realms are fundamentally one mind from beginning to end, and birth-and-death and nirvana ultimately have no two boundaries.

However, returning to the ultimate source of Great Awakening requires the accumulation of merit before it can be attained; as one follows the current of the long dream, it cannot be opened all at once.
This is why the traces left by the Sages are sometimes distant and sometimes near, and why the teachings they established sometimes decline and sometimes flourish.
As for the World-Honored Muni manifesting here in this Sahā world to admonish against the five evils and exhort toward goodness,
and Amitābha Tathāgata dwelling in that Land of Peaceful Nurturing to lead the nine grades of beings toward rebirth— such expedient traces are beyond full description.
This Land of Ultimate Bliss now elucidated is truly the profound depth of the fruition of responsive vows and practice;

it is the far-reaching manifestation of the merit of realized virtue. Its eighteen aspects of perfect purity transcend and surpass the three realms, while its five faculties and marks of excellence do not even equal those of the six heavens.
The rare fragrance of the Dharma-flavor nourishes both body and mind; who, then, suffers the afflictions of hunger by day or thirst by night?
The fragrant breeze of the Jade Forest is always temperate and pleasant; fundamentally, there is no distress of winter’s cold or summer’s heat.
The assembly of immortals gathers together to bathe at the Lotus Pond of Eight Virtues; thus they forever part from the wrinkles of time that are most loathsome.
Following one another as noble companions, they travel afar to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, leaving behind this sorrowful toil that is so difficult to console.
How much more so when one hears the resonance of the Dharma and enters into signlessness, beholds the Buddha’s radiance and awakens to non-arising?

Because one awakens to non-arising, there is nothing that does not arise; because one enters into formlessness, there is nothing that does not take form. Utterly pure and utterly blissful, it is beyond the reach of mind or thought;
boundless and limitless, how could words ever exhaust its description?
Such a pure land is praised and commended by the Buddhas of the ten directions and is the dwelling place where the noble assemblies of the three vehicles roam.
Yet, if one carefully examines the intent behind the Tathāgata’s praise and exhortation, it is because he wishes to gather in and protect those of middling and inferior faculties.
The Sahā world is a place of mixed evils where one frequently regresses due to conditions;
the precious land of Sukhāvatī is a realm of pure goodness where there is only progress and no regression.
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says:

"Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, when first learning this Dharma and desiring to seek right faith, find their minds timid and weak. Because they dwell in this Sahā world, they fear that they will not be able to constantly encounter the Buddhas to personally receive them and make offerings; they dread that the mind of faith will be difficult to accomplish and thus intend to retreat."

You should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to gather in and protect those with faith; namely, by virtue of the causal conditions of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, one will, according to one's vows, be reborn in the buddha-fields of other directions, where one constantly beholds the Buddha and is forever freed from the evil realms.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, dedicates the roots of goodness they have cultivated, and vows to be born in that world, they shall immediately attain rebirth there."

Because one constantly beholds the Buddha, there shall never be any regression; if one contemplates that Buddha’s *tathatā-dharmakāya* and practices it with constant diligence, one will ultimately attain birth in the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

"Although all ordinary beings may practice mindfulness of the Buddha, as long as they have not yet attained the stage of 'Ten Understandings' (*daśa-vyavasthāna*), their essential nature remains subject to regression.
If they dwell in a defiled land, they will fall back even upon encountering the four conditions for regression;
however, if they are born in the Western Land, because of the presence of those four conditions [of support], they shall never regress."
Regarding the four conditions:
first, because of long life and freedom from illness, one does not regress;
whereas in a defiled land, due to short life and much illness, one regresses.
Second, one does not regress because of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who are perfect and virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), as the Sūtra says:
"Because one meets with such superior and virtuous people in one place.
In contrast, one regresses in a defiled land (*sāpatti-bhūmi*) due to the abundance of evil spiritual friends (*pāpamitra*).
Third, because there are no women and the objects of the six sense faculties are all conditions for advancing on the path, one does not regress; as the sutra says:
"Upon seeing forms with the eye, one immediately gives rise to the bodhicitta," and so forth;
whereas in a defiled land, one regresses because of the presence of women.
Fourth, because there is only a wholesome mind, one does not regress; as the Sūtra says:
"There is not even a space the size of a hair-tip where one might conceive of committing evil.
In the defiled lands, however, because of the presence of unwholesome minds and neutral (avyākṛta) minds, one regresses.
Furthermore, both of those two sūtras state:
"Those who attain rebirth there all achieve non-retrogression.

They do not say that only those who have already attained non-retrogression can attain rebirth there; it is just as in this world, where one who possesses the three types of feeling, if born in that land, will have neither painful nor neutral feelings, but only pleasant feelings.
In brief, from the first bhūmi upward, compassion and vows are sovereign and there is nothing that cannot be brought forth; what further need is there to exhort them?

From the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-avakalana*) onward, the spiritual lineage is determined and there is no longer any regression from compassion, so they are not the primary object of such encouragement.

As for those prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), their resolve is not yet firm; they rise and fall according to conditions, loathing defilement and longing for purity; therefore, the Buddha exhorts and gathers them in.
In the Western Land, life is long, and one may attain the stages [of bodhisattvahood] through a single lifetime of practice;
in the Sahā world, life is short, and even after many kalpas of arduous effort, one may still regress.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"One kalpa in this Sahā world is equivalent to one day and night in the Western World of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī).

In this manner, even up to a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, one kalpa in the final world is equivalent to one day and night in the realm of the Tathāgata Bhadrasena in the World of Supreme Lotuses."
The instruction on generating the aspiration has been briefly summarized thus.
Second, regarding the determination of the location of that land:
the Buddha-fields are perfectly interfused; fundamentally, there is neither east nor west.
The triggers of the mechanism are manifold, and only then do "this" and "that" appear.
From this, let us tentatively discuss how the locations of those realms differ according to the distinctions between the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles.
If one relies upon the One Vehicle, the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is subsumed within the Flower Treasury World-Ocean. Why is this?
Because these lands of the ten Buddhas are perfectly interfused and ineffable, and because that which is perceived by the causal stage of Samantabhadra is without limits.
If categorized according to the Three Vehicles, the Pure Lands of the Western Quarter generally comprise four lands:
first, the Dharma-nature Land; second, the Land of Realized Reward;
[third, the Shared Land; and fourth, the Transformation Land].
Third, the land of enjoyment;
fourth, the land of transformation.
Among these, the land of the dharma-nature and the land of true retribution consist of a single flavor of bliss that pervades the entire dharma-realm, beyond the comprehension of others.

The enjoyment [buddha-fields] and transformation [buddha-fields] are attained through the fulfillment of vows and the ripening of karmic conditions; they are praised according to the capacities of sentient beings and can only be pointed out by direction.
Thus, the *Sūtra of the Lesser Immeasurable Life* says:
"To the west of here, passing beyond a hundred trillion buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī."
Now, regarding that realm—whether pure or impure—it shall be briefly elucidated through four pairs of contrasts to reveal its gradations:
namely, the contrast between cause and fruit;
and the contrast between the univocal and the non-univocal.
Because the pure and the mixed are relative to one another;
because right concentration and non-right concentration are relative to one another.
As for what was said regarding cause and fruit being relative to one another:

That is to say, the abodes of bodhisattvas from the stage of *vajra* downwards are called lands of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), but they are not called pure lands (*śuddhabhūmi*), because they have not yet abandoned the afflictions that are the fruits of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Only the dwelling place of a Buddha is called a pure land, because all defiled afflictions have been extinguished without remainder.
Based on this meaning, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states:
"The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in the retribution of their fruits; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land."
"All sentient beings, having briefly dwelt in the retribution realm, ascend to the Vajra Ground and reside in the Pure Land.
Second, regarding the contrast between the "exclusive" and the "non-exclusive":

This means that the dwelling places of Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward are designated as "Pure Lands" (*śuddhakṣetra*), because they exclusively transcend the three realms (*tridhātu*) and because they fully possess the fourfold sense of "exclusivity.

All dwelling places from the seventh stage downward are not yet called Pure Lands, because they do not exclusively transcend the three realms; or, even for those who transcend the three realms through the power of their vows, they do not fully possess the fourfold exclusivity—namely, exclusive bliss, exclusive purity, exclusive freedom from calamity, and exclusive sovereignty.

When manifesting from the seventh stage downward, there are times when a resultant indeterminate mind (*vipāka-avyākṛta-citta*) arises; because the four functions of the manas are active at that time, it is not exclusively pure, nor is it produced solely by the power of mundane wholesome dharmas.
The commentary states:

"Riding upon the wholesome is called 'transcending the world. From the eighth stage upward, up to the stage of Buddhahood, is termed "transcending the world. Transcendent phenomena (lokottara-dharma) are the counterpart to worldly phenomena (laukika-dharma), and transcendent phenomena serve as the antidote to worldly phenomena.

It takes the four conditions as its characteristic because this pure land arises from the emergence of virtuous merits; it does not take the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) as its cause, and so forth, as explained at length.
Third, regarding the gate of the contrast between the pure and the mixed:
A place where ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles dwell together cannot be called a pure world;
only the birthplaces of bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (mahābhūmi) can be designated as pure worlds.
Because that is not purely pure, whereas this is purely pure, it is on the basis of this meaning that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The worlds are immeasurable, and there are two kinds:
namely, the pure and the impure."

In a pure world-system, there are no hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts; nor does it belong to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. It is inhabited solely by a multitude of bodhisattvas, and for this reason it is called a "pure world-system."

When a bodhisattva has already entered the third stage, by the power of their vows they take birth there; no ordinary beings, nor śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—whether ordinary or non-ordinary—can be born there, except for bodhisattvas who are non-ordinary.
The commentary states:

"This third ground is the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Because it is the third ground among the sevenfold doors of the grounds—namely, the Ground of Pure Superior Intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*)—it subsumes thirteen stages and is established as seven types of grounds."
This is because it is exactly as explained in that treatise.
Fourth, regarding the gate of contrasting right concentration and non-right concentration:
the state where the three groups of sentient beings who lack right concentration give rise to suffering is called a defiled land (saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra).

Only the dwelling place of those in the group of right determination (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi) is called a Pure Land; within it there are also śrāvakas of the four fruits, and even ordinary persons with the four doubts, though it lacks only those in the group of wrong determination (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi) and the group of no fixed determination (aniyata-rāśi).
Regarding the phrase "right concentration," etc.,
this is a general statement that the realm of sentient beings consists, in brief,
of three groups (*rāśi*). As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"Any sentient beings who are born in that land shall all abide in the stage of those destined for right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Why is this?
Because in that Buddha-land, there are no groups of the wrong determination (*mithyātva-niyāma*) nor of the undetermined (*aniyata-niyāma*)."
What are the characteristics of these three types?
To state them collectively: those who are icchantikas belong to the group of the definitely false;

those from the stage of the "summit" (mūrdhan) of the two vehicles upward, and those from the bodhisattva's first stage of "initial resolve" (prathamacittotpāda-vihāra) upward, are judged to be the definitely right.
If one has already entered [the path] but has not yet reached its stage, they belong to the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).
Being certain not to regress and never severing the roots of goodness—this is what is meant by the meaning of the "fixed-in-rightness group" (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) is of two kinds:
first, innate right concentration;
second, acquired right concentration.

Among the five types of lineages (*gotra*), those of the bodhisattva lineage do not rely upon the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) or the severing of the roots of goodness; these are called the "original birth" group of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktvaniyatarāśi*).

Those of the two vehicles' lineage and those of indeterminate lineage can commit the five heinous crimes and sever the roots of goodness; at the moment they sever the roots of goodness, they are called the group fixed in error (*mithyātvaniyatarāśi*).
These same individuals, after reconnecting the roots of goodness but before entering [the path], constitute the indeterminate group (*aniyatarāśi*).

Once one has entered [the path], there are three grades: those who enter with an originally superior faculty immediately achieve right determination; those with middling faculties reach the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) and achieve right determination; and those with inferior faculties reach the stage of "Summit" (mūrdhan) and each achieves right determination;
all others belong to the category of the indeterminate.

If a person of indeterminate lineage directly turns toward and enters the Mahāyāna, they must practice with faith for ten thousand kalpas; only when their faith is perfected do they become fixed in the right determination.
The *Awakening of Faith* clarifies this very meaning, which refers to those who achieve the stage of the "definite group" (*niyata-rāśi*) through cultivation.

As for those of the original Bodhisattva lineage who enter directly toward the Mahāyāna, at the very moment of their initial entry, they attain permanent non-retrogression and do not fall into the evil destinies by the power of karma.

According to this, upon entering the stage of the ten faiths, one attains non-retrogression; this differs from the previously mentioned persons of indeterminate nature. Such explanations as these all pertain to the defiled lands.

Regarding those who attain birth in that Pure Land: those of the two vehicles with fixed natures do not attain rebirth there; they may only attain rebirth after the state of nirvana without remainder.

Among those with indeterminate natures, all three grades of persons who have resolved their minds shall attain birth there. At the moment of birth, they immediately enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), because they are sustained by the power of external conditions.
The brief meaning of the threefold classification is thus.
Now, this sutra speaks of the Land of Immeasurable Life; it is explained as a Pure Land according to the fourth category. Why is this so?

This is because [the Buddha] desires that neither the great nor the small be excluded, and that both ordinary beings and sages be led together to be born in superior realms and to proceed toward the Great Way.
As stated in the following passage:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the people in my land do not dwell in the stage of certainty and necessarily reach extinction, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Furthermore, it says:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any among the śrāvakas in my land who are able to calculate and know their number, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
This is stated at length in the sūtra.
As for the statement in the treatise:
"Women and those with impaired faculties, as well as those of the two vehicles' lineage, do not produce [the Buddha-nature]," this refers to those of a fixed lineage.

It does not refer to śrāvakas of indeterminate capacity or those of the nature of seeking quiescence after they have entered the nirvana without remainder and subsequently resolve to generate the Great Mind.
To exclude these [other interpretations], the term "those of the two vehicles' lineage" is used;
by this reasoning, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "women and those with impaired faculties," it means that at the time of birth there, they are neither female nor have impaired faculties; it does not mean that women and others cannot attain rebirth there, for it is seen that even Vaidehī attained rebirth there.
However, the *Drum-Svara-Rāja Dhāraṇī Sūtra* states:
"The father of Amitābha Buddha was named King Candra-vimala-cakra-vartin, and his mother was named Viśiṣṭa-nayanā," and so forth, as explained at length. Regarding this, some say:

"This describes the transformation land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*) where a transformation Buddha resides, whereas that which is discussed in the [Abhidharma] treatises refers to the enjoyment land (*saṃbhoga-kṣetra*)."
Others say: "This dharma-gate is the father and mother [of all teachings], as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*.
For this reason, there is no contradiction.

The pure lands explained in the four preceding sections are all accomplished through the vows and practices of the Tathāgata; they are not produced by the individual power of those born therein. Unlike the external vessel-world of the defiled land, which is formed solely by the bitter fruits of sentient beings' karma, these are therefore collectively termed "Pure Lands."
Third, the clarification of the affliction of doubt and difficulty.
Within this, first the object of doubt is clarified;
next, the counteractive thought for doubt is clarified.
The following clarifies the superiority and inferiority of those born from transformation and from the womb.
Regarding the statement "clarifying the objects of doubt," it is as the subsequent text says:

"If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of doubt, cultivate merit and vow to be born in that land, yet do not understand the Buddha’s wisdom—the inconceivable wisdom, the incomparable wisdom, the vast Mahāyāna wisdom, and the peerless, matchless, supreme, and preeminent wisdom—and harbor doubts and lack faith in these various forms of wisdom; nevertheless, they still believe in sin and merit, practice wholesome deeds, and vow to be born in that land."
"These sentient beings are born in that palace and do not hear of the Three Jewels for five hundred years; therefore, it is called a 'borderland.
This is explained at length.
The phrase "the Buddha's wisdom" is the general heading.
The four subsequent lines each manifest one of the four wisdoms.

"Inconceivable wisdom" refers to the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done); this wisdom can perform inconceivable deeds, such as manifesting a body no more than sixteen feet tall while no one is able to see its crown;
or manifesting the size of a single pore without increasing it, yet pervading the worlds of the ten directions.
To recite the name even for a single thought-moment eternally extinguishes the heavy sins of many kalpas;
to contemplate its virtues for ten thoughts can produce superior retribution beyond this world.
Such matters are beyond the scope of human measurement; therefore, it is called inconceivable wisdom.

The "incalculable wisdom" is the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). This wisdom observes incalculable objects, namely that all phenomena are like illusions and like dreams; they are neither existent nor non-existent, transcending words and beyond thought. They cannot be measured by those who pursue words; therefore, it is called the incalculable wisdom.

The "vast wisdom of the Mahāyāna" is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). This wisdom is vast in its deliverance, differing from that of the Hīnayāna; it means that by roaming within non-self, there is no "not-self," and because there is no "not-self," there is no failure to include all equally.

By means of this power of wisdom of identical essence, it universally sustains infinite sentient beings, leading them all completely and equally to unsurpassed *bodhi*. For this reason, it is called the "vast wisdom of the Mahāyāna."

The peerless, incomparable, and most supreme wisdom is precisely the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Only when the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is first transformed does one return to the source of the mind; therein, all objective realms are perfectly reflected without exception, and this is therefore called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

This single Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom possesses five kinds of excellence. Like the Body of Liberation, which both the Two Vehicles and Buddhas attain in common, this Mirror Wisdom is precisely the Dharma-body; it is not shared by them, and is therefore called "unequaled"—this is the first excellence.
Just as the previous three wisdoms are attained gradually by Bodhisattvas, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is realized instantaneously only by a Buddha, with no other category of being possessing it;

thus it is called "peerless"—this is the second excellence. It is the most supreme among inconceivable wisdoms, the highest above incomparable wisdoms, and superior to the vast wisdom of the Mahāyāna; these constitute the third, fourth, and fifth excellences. Therefore, it is named "unequaled," "peerless," and "supreme victorious wisdom," which reveals the object of delusion for the four types of doubt.
Next, to clarify the characteristics of the antidotes for doubt:

suppose there is a person whose nature is not upright, who is deceptively clever and arrogant, and whose aspiration for the Path is slight; such a person fails to understand the four wisdoms and gives rise to four doubts.
The first is doubting the activities performed by the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom).
That is to say, the same sutra states that "by ten recollections of the Buddha, one attains birth in that land. Because they do not understand this, they give rise to doubt and say:
"As the Buddha’s sutras state:
'The paths of good and evil karma—the demerit and merit—do not perish.'"
Since heavy [karmic] obstructions are logically consistent with being impediments,

how can it be that one who has committed every kind of evil throughout a lifetime can, by means of ten recitations alone, extinguish all such sins, thereby attain rebirth there, enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), forever leave the three miserable realms, and ultimately never regress?
Furthermore, since beginningless time, various afflictions have arisen, binding one to the three realms and entangling one within them.
How can one not sever the afflictions of the two wheels, yet directly transcend the three realms through ten recitations?

To remedy such erroneous thoughts and doubts, it is therefore called "inconceivable wisdom" (acintya-jñāna). To manifest that the Buddha’s wisdom possesses great power, he is able to make the near distant and the distant near;
to make the heavy light and the light heavy.

Although this matter is indeed real, it is not an object of discursive thought; therefore, one should directly and reverently believe what the sūtras teach, rather than attempting to fathom it with one's own limited and superficial consciousness.

If one wishes to give rise to faith, it should be explained by means of an illustration: for example, suppose there were a pile of firewood a thousand years old, a hundred li in height; even if measured by the size of a single bean, if set ablaze, it would all be consumed in a single day.
One might say:
"How can a stack of firewood accumulated over a thousand years be exhausted in a single day?

Or again, consider a cripple who, through his own diligent efforts, takes many days to travel one *yojana*; yet if he boards another's ship, he can reach a thousand *li* in a single day by means of the wind’s power. One might then say:
"How can a cripple travel a thousand li in a single day?
Even the power of a worldly boatman can accomplish such an inconceivable feat;
how much more so, then, could the power of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, not perform an inconceivable deed?
This is the remedy for the first doubt.
As for the second doubt, it refers to doubting the object perceived by the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
In the sūtras, the Buddha’s wisdom is praised as follows:
"The wisdom of wondrous observation [sees] that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent; it is far removed from the two extremes and does not cling to the middle way.
Because they do not understand this, doubt arises, and they say:
"As we observe and weigh things now, when an object is heavy it sinks, and when an object is light it must rise."
If one says that what is light does not rise and what is heavy does not sink, such a speaker speaks of words but lacks meaning.
One should know that phenomena born of causes and conditions are likewise: if they are truly not non-existent, they follow from existence;
if they are not existent, they belong to non-existence.

If one says that it is not non-existent yet cannot be said to exist, and is not existent yet does not fall into non-existence, then it is like something that is heavy yet does not sink, or light yet does not rise; thus we know this is a case of speaking of existence while its reality is non-existence.
To evaluate things in this manner is to fall into the extremes:
either one clings to the dependent nature as truly existent, falling into the extreme of superimposition;
or one clings to that which arises through conditions as being empty and non-existent, falling into the extreme of denial.
Some reckon that conventional existence and ultimate emptiness are both negated, falling into the discourse of contradiction;
others reckon that there is neither existence nor non-existence, clinging to a single middle point, and thus falling into the discourse of ignorance.
As the *Śāstra* states:
"To say 'neither existent nor non-existent' is the discourse of the deluded.

To counteract such erroneous conceptualizations and attachments, the inconceivable wisdom (*acintya-jñāna*) is established; this is intended to reveal that all phenomena are profoundly deep, transcending words, beyond thought, and cannot be sought after through deliberation or measured by conceptualization, nor grasped according to their literal expression.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
"What is the profound and difficult-to-perceive dharma? It refers to all dharmas. Why is this?"

The first most profound and difficult-to-perceive dharma is what is called the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena (*dharma*): it transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and exceeds the path of words and speech.
Nevertheless, because verbal expression serves as a correct basis, it can then be grasped, observed, and realized; therefore, all phenomena are profound and difficult to perceive.
This serves as the remedy for the second doubt.
As for the third doubt, it refers to doubting the intention to provide relief through the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and so forth.
As stated in the same sutra:
"All sentient beings possess a mind; all who possess a mind shall attain bodhi.
Because they do not understand this, they give rise to doubt and say:

"If it is said that 'all sentient beings have Buddha-nature' and that 'one shall deliver all sentient beings, causing them to attain unsurpassed bodhi,' then although sentient beings are numerous, they must eventually come to an end. Consequently, the final Buddha would lack the virtue of benefiting others because there would be no one to be transformed; thus, he would ultimately fail to become a Buddha due to the deficiency of merit."
"It is illogical that there is merit in the absence of others;
likewise, it is impossible for Buddhahood to be attained through the lack of merit.
Holding such erroneous views, they slander the Mahāyāna and do not believe in the principle of universal equality and deliverance.

To remedy such narrow and limited doubts and attachments, the vast wisdom of the Mahāyāna is established. It is called "Mahāyāna" because it clarifies that while the Buddha’s wisdom carries nothing itself, it carries all beings, leading them all into the remainderless nirvāṇa;
and it is called "vast wisdom" because that which it carries is limitless and boundless.
The reason for this is that because space is boundless, sentient beings are beyond measure;
because the three periods of time have no limits, birth and death have no beginning or end.
Since sentient beings have neither beginning nor end, the Buddhas likewise have neither beginning nor end.
If it were the case that there are Buddhas who first achieve enlightenment, then prior to them there would have been no Buddha-fruit and no holy teaching;
because there would be no holy teaching, there would be no perfuming by hearing (*śrutavāsanā*);
and if one were to become a Buddha despite the absence of perfuming by hearing, this would mean having a fruit without a cause, which is a mere word without reality.
By this principle, the Buddhas have no beginning.

Although they truly have no beginning, there is not a single Buddha who was not originally an ordinary being; although all were originally ordinary beings, they are successively without beginning. By this analogy, one should know that sentient beings have no end.
Although they truly have no end, there is not a single person who will not eventually become a Buddha; although all will eventually become Buddhas, they are successively without end.

Therefore, one should believe that the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) has nothing it does not deliver and is not limited; thus, the vast wisdom of the Mahāyāna is established. This serves as the remedy for the third doubt.
The fourth doubt concerns the meaning of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) universally illuminating all objects.
Why does this doubt arise?
It is because one speaks as follows:
"Because space is infinite, the worlds are also infinite;
because the worlds are infinite, sentient beings are also infinite;
because sentient beings are infinite, the distinctions of their mental states, faculties, desires, natures, and so forth, are all without limit."
How can one come to know this exhaustively? Is it through gradual cultivation that one comes to know it, or is it through sudden, instantaneous illumination without cultivation?

If it were through sudden, instantaneous illumination without cultivation, then all ordinary beings should equally attain such illumination, for they are equally uncultivated and there is no differing cause.
If one were to gradually cultivate [this knowledge] until finally attaining exhaustive knowledge, then all objects would not be limitless; for it is illogical that the limitless could have an end.
Thus, whether one proceeds or regresses, neither position is established. How, then, can there be universal illumination, which is designated as "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*)?

To resolve these two points of doubt and difficulty, the peerless, incomparable, and supreme transcendent wisdom is established; it is intended to clarify that this Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) surpasses the other three wisdoms and has no equal, existing alone beyond the two truths as the non-dual.

Beyond the two barriers, it is transcendent and without opening; one can only respond with reverent faith and must not attempt to measure it through comparison. Therefore, it is called the Supreme Victorious Wisdom.
How does one give rise to this reverent faith?
For example, just as the worlds are boundless yet do not exist outside of space, so too the myriad objects are infinite yet all enter within the single mind.

Buddha-wisdom is free from marks and returns to the source of the single mind; wisdom and the single mind are thus blended as one without duality. Since initial awakening is identical to original awakening, there are no myriad objects that exist outside of wisdom.
By this principle, there is no object that is not exhausted, yet it is not limited, because boundless wisdom illumines boundless objects.
As the *Awakening of Faith* says:

"All objects are originally the one mind, free from conceptualization. Because sentient beings falsely perceive objects, the mind appears to have limitations; because they falsely give rise to signs and thoughts that do not accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are unable to comprehend them."

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are free from the marks of perception and are omnipresent; because their minds are true, this is the nature of all phenomena. Their own essence illuminates all delusive dharmas, possessing the function of great wisdom and immeasurable skillful means. According to what each sentient being should understand, they are able to reveal the meaning of all dharmas; therefore, they are named "Omniscient Wisdom" (sarvākārajñatā).
This is the peerless, incomparable, and supreme transcendent wisdom; because there is nothing seen, there is nothing not seen. In this way, it serves as the antidote to the fourth doubt.

If one does not grasp the intended meaning but instead takes the words at face value, both the positions of "having limits" and "being limitless" are fraught with faults; therefore, we provisionally speak of the meaning of "limitlessness" based on the perspective that there are no limits.
If a person does not resolve these four doubts, although they may be born in that land, they will reside in a border region.

However, if there is someone who, though not yet clearly understanding, can briefly describe the realms of the four aforementioned wisdoms and modestly acknowledge their own limitations; whose mental eye has not yet opened, yet looks up to and dedicates themselves to the Tathāgata with single-minded submission and faith—such people, according to the grade of their practice, will be reborn in that land and will not dwell in a border region.
Those born in those borderlands constitute a distinct category and are not subsumed within the nine grades.
Therefore, one should not give rise to groundless doubts.
Next, to clarify the superiority and inferiority of those born there through transformation or from a womb, it is as stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*:
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda and the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Do you see all the subtle, exquisite, pure, and natural objects within that land, from the ground upward to the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens? Do you see them all?"
Ānanda replied, "Indeed!
I have seen it."
"Have you not heard how the Buddha of Immeasurable Life proclaims his great voice throughout all worlds to transform sentient beings?
Ānanda replied, "Indeed, I have."
"I have heard it.

"Do you also see how the people of that land, riding in palaces made of the seven treasures and measuring a hundred thousand yojanas, travel everywhere throughout the ten directions without obstruction to make offerings to the Buddhas?"
He replied, "I have seen them. [The Buddha asked:
"Among the people of that land, do you also see those who are born from a womb?"
He replied, "I have seen them.

[The Buddha asked,] "As for those born from wombs, the palaces in which they dwell are either one hundred yojanas or five hundred yojanas in extent; within each of these, they experience various pleasures, just as in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, all of which arise spontaneously."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what cause and by what condition do the people of that land undergo birth from a womb or birth by transformation?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of doubt, cultivate various meritorious virtues and vow to be born in that land, yet do not understand the Buddha’s wisdom, his inconceivable wisdom, his incomparable wisdom, his vast Mahāyāna wisdom, and his peerless, matchless, supreme, and most excellent wisdom; if they harbor doubts and lack faith in these various forms of wisdom, yet still believe in sin and merit and practice the roots of goodness, vowing to be born in that land."

These sentient beings are born in those palaces with a lifespan of five hundred years; they constantly do not see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, and do not see the assembly of holy Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas. For this reason, they are said to be "womb-born" (garbhaja) in that land.

If there are sentient beings who clearly believe in the Buddha’s wisdom, up to and including his supreme wisdom, and perform various meritorious deeds, dedicating them with a faithful mind, these sentient beings will be spontaneously born by transformation within lotus flowers made of the seven treasures, sitting in the full-lotus posture. In a mere instant, their physical marks, radiance, wisdom, and merit will be fully perfected, just like those of the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Maitreya!

When great bodhisattvas from other buddha-fields resolve to see the Buddha Amitāyus, to pay him respectful homage and offerings, as well as his assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, those bodhisattvas, upon the end of their lives, will attain rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Life, spontaneously manifesting by transformation within flowers made of the seven precious jewels.
Maitreya, you should know this:
those who are born by transformation possess superior wisdom;

whereas those who are born from a womb all lack wisdom. For five hundred years, they constantly fail to see the Buddha, hear the sutras and Dharma, or encounter the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. Having no means to make offerings to the Buddha, they do not know the ritual methods of the bodhisattvas and cannot cultivate meritorious virtues. You should know that these people, during their previous lives, lacked wisdom due to the influence of doubt and confusion.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:

"Suppose, for example, there were a secure prison belonging to a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin-rāja), adorned in various ways, furnished with couches and canopies, and hung with silken banners and streamers."

If any of the minor princes should incur the offense of the king, the king would immediately take them into his inner palace and bind them with golden chains; yet he would provide them with food, drink, clothing, bedding, flowers, incense, and music, just like a wheel-turning monarch, so that they lacked for nothing.
"What do you think? Would these princes take pleasure in that place? He replied, "No!"
"However, by means of various skillful methods, they seek great powers in order to escape and emerge from it themselves.
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"These sentient beings are also like this; because they harbor doubts regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, they are born in those palaces of the seven treasures through gestation, where there are no punishments, nor even a single thought of evil."

However, during those five hundred years, they do not see the Triple Gem nor can they make offerings or cultivate the roots of goodness; taking this as their suffering, even though other pleasures exist, they find no joy in that place.

If these sentient beings recognize their fundamental transgressions, deeply repent and reproach themselves, and seek to leave that place, they will immediately attain their wish and proceed to the abode of Amitāyus Buddha to pay respectful homage and make offerings; they shall also be able to travel everywhere to the abodes of immeasurable and innumerable other Buddhas to cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues.
Maitreya, you should know that any bodhisattva who gives rise to doubt will lose a great benefit; therefore, one should have clear faith in the unsurpassed wisdom of all Buddhas.
The Tathāgata’s mantras do not produce strange or anomalous results; once regret has set in, it is difficult to turn back. How can one not be cautious!

Fourth, regarding the manifestation of the causes and conditions for rebirth: generally speaking, all that is taught as the cause for rebirth does not merely evoke the adornment of the primary retribution (the body), but also evokes the purity of the secondary retribution (the land). This is solely because of the power of the Tathāgata’s original vows; one experiences these enjoyments according to what is received, rather than through the power of the causal force of one's own karma. Therefore, this is called the "cause for rebirth."

The characteristics of these causes are numerous in the sūtras and śāstras; for instance, the *Contemplation Sūtra* explains sixteen contemplations, while the *Treatise on Rebirth* explains the practices of the five gates.
Now, following this *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, the causes of the three grades are explained; within the superior grade, there are five phrases:
First, leaving home and abandoning desire to become a śramaṇa, which reveals the skillful means for generating the correct cause;
second, giving rise to the bodhicitta, which clarifies the correct cause itself;
third, single-mindedly recollecting that Buddha, which clarifies the cultivation of contemplation.
Fourth, performing various meritorious deeds is the clear arising of practice; this contemplation and these practices constitute auxiliary karma.
Fifth, making the vow to be born in that land.
This one is the vow, while the preceding four are the practices; it is through the union of practice and vow that birth [in the Pure Land] is attained.
Regarding the exposition of the middle grade, there are four points:
first, although one may not become a śramaṇa, one should resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta; this clarifies the direct cause.
Second, the vow to be born in that land.
The preceding practice and this vow, combined, constitute the cause.
Within the category of the "inferior grade," two types of persons are described; within each of these two types, there are three phrases.
Regarding the three factors for the first type of person:
first, even if one is unable to perform various meritorious deeds, one should resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta; this clarifies the primary cause.
Second, even for as little as ten recitations, one should focus single-mindedly on that Buddha; this constitutes the auxiliary practice.
Third, they vow to be born in that land.
With this vow as the precursor and these factors combined as the cause, this clarifies the person of indeterminate lineage.
Regarding the second type of person, there are three statements:

First, hearing the profound Dharma and rejoicing with faith and delight; this phrase also reveals the primary cause for generating the resolve [for enlightenment], yet it is mentioned here specifically to distinguish it from the previous case by emphasizing deep faith.
Second, even for a single moment of thought, recollecting that Buddha; this constitutes the auxiliary cause.
Because those former individuals lacked deep faith, it was necessary for them to have ten recitations;
because this person possesses deep faith, they may not necessarily complete ten recitations.
Third, one must possess a sincere mind and aspire to be born in that land.
This vow is the precursor, and its harmonious integration constitutes the cause; this refers to those of the Bodhisattva lineage.
As the Sūtras explain it thus, the present text briefly elucidates its characteristics, which are twofold:
first, the clarification of the direct cause (*hetu*); second, the clarification of the auxiliary conditions (*pratyaya*).

What is called the "correct cause" refers to the generation of the unsurpassed bodhicitta; that is, not aspiring for worldly wealth and pleasure, nor for the enlightenment of the two vehicles, but rather the Bodhisattva’s single-minded vow for the enlightenment of the three bodies (trikāya-bodhi), which is termed the unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Although this is the general outline, there are two types within it:
first, generating the mind of enlightenment in accordance with specific phenomena;
second, generating the mind of enlightenment in conformity with ultimate principle.
Regarding "acting in accordance with things": afflictions are innumerable, yet one vows to sever them all;
wholesome dharmas are immeasurable, yet one vows to cultivate them all;
sentient beings are boundless, yet one vows to deliver them all.

Regarding these three matters, one makes a firm resolution and vow: the first is the direct cause for the Tathāgata’s virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); the second is the direct cause for the Tathāgata’s virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); and the third mind is the direct cause for the virtue of gratitude (*anugraha-guṇa*). These three virtues combined constitute unsurpassed bodhi; that is, these three minds together serve as the cause for unsurpassed bodhi.
Although cause and effect differ, their breadth and length are equal in measure; they are identical without omission, for there is nothing not encompassed.

As the sutra says: "The initial resolve and the ultimate goal are not two different things. Of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult: to seek to deliver others before one has delivered oneself. Therefore, I pay homage to the generation of the bodhicitta.
Although the ultimate fruition of this mind is bodhi, its provisional blossoming reward lies in the Pure Land.

The reason for this is that the magnitude of the bodhicitta is vast and boundless, long-lasting and infinite; therefore, it can evoke a vast and limitless environment of reliance—the Pure Land—and a long-lasting, immeasurable primary retribution of lifespan. Since nothing but the bodhicitta can withstand such results, this mind is said to be their direct cause. This clarifies the characteristics of generating the mind according to specific circumstances.

Regarding what is called "arousing the mind in accordance with principle": one has faith and understanding that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams—neither existent nor non-existent, beyond words and transcending thought.

Relying on this faith and understanding, one arouses the vast and great mind; although one does not perceive the existence of afflictions or wholesome dharmas, one does not negate that which is to be severed or cultivated. Therefore, while one vows to sever all [afflictions] and cultivate [wholesome dharmas], one does not contradict the samādhi of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*); and while one vows to deliver immeasurable sentient beings, one does not maintain the notion of a deliverer or those to be delivered. Thus, one is able to accord with emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*).
As the Sūtra says:
"In this way, though one brings immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa," and so on, as explained at length.
Therefore, such an arousal of the mind is inconceivable; this clarifies the characteristics of an arousal of the mind that accords with principle.
Generating the mind [of enlightenment] in accordance with specific circumstances carries the possibility of regression; even those of indeterminate nature can generate it.
Generating the mind in accordance with principle is irreversible; only those of the bodhisattva nature can generate it.
The merit of generating the mind in this way is boundless; even if all Buddhas were to expound it throughout the exhaustion of kalpas, those merits could not be fully exhausted.
Such, in brief, is the characteristic of the true cause.
Next, the auxiliary causes are explained.
There are many types of auxiliary causes; as they frequently appear in the sūtras and śāstras, there is no need for a detailed exposition here—one should understand each according to those sources.
For now, we shall clarify the ten recitations of the lower grade. Within the single phrase regarding the ten recitations of the middle and lower grades in this sūtra, two meanings are contained:
This refers to the explicit meaning and the implicit meaning.

Regarding the implicit meaning, this is explained in contrast to the third pair—the fruit of the purely pure land—with respect to the merit of the ten recitations of the lower grade. This is as stated in the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
"At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed [the Buddha], saying:"

"As the Buddha has taught regarding the merits and benefits of Amitābha Buddha, if one can maintain ten consecutive recitations of that Buddha without interruption, one will immediately attain rebirth there."
"How should one practice mindfulness?

The Buddha said, "It is not the mindfulness of an ordinary person, nor is it unwholesome mindfulness, nor is it mindfulness associated with the fetters and afflictions. By being fully endowed with such mindfulness, one will attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss."
There are ten kinds of mindfulness; what are these ten?

First, one should always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and not disparage the conduct of any sentient being; if one disparages their conduct, one will ultimately not attain rebirth there.
Second, one should deeply give rise to a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings and eliminate all intent to harm.
Third, they give rise to the mind that protects the Dharma, not sparing even their own body or life, and never engendering slander toward any teaching;
fourth, they develop a mind of firm resolve within the practice of patience;
fifth, their profound mind is pure, and they do not crave gain or offerings.
Sixth, to resolve upon the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-citta*) and to maintain constant mindfulness of it day after day without neglect or forgetfulness;
seventh, to give rise to a heart of reverence toward all sentient beings, eliminate the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), and speak with humility;
eighth, to not develop a mind of attachment or relish for worldly talk.
Ninth, they draw near to the factors of enlightenment, deeply generating the causes and conditions for various roots of goodness, and remain far removed from a mind that is agitated and distracted;
tenth, they contemplate the Buddha with right mindfulness, eliminating all doubts.
The commentary states:
Since these ten recollections are not [the domain] of ordinary beings, one should know that only Bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward are able to fully possess these ten recollections.
In the Pure Land, these serve as the causes for those of the lower grade; this constitutes the ten recitations of the hidden meaning.
As for the characteristics of the ten recitations of the explicit meaning, they are explained in relation to the fourth pair of purities.
As stated in the *Contemplation Sūtra*:

"Regarding those born in the lowest of the lower grades: there may be sentient beings who have committed unwholesome deeds, the five heinous crimes, and the ten evil acts, being fully possessed of all manner of unwholesomeness."
"At the time of death, one encounters a virtuous friend who expounds the sublime Dharma and instructs one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

If one is unable to practice mindfulness, one should instead recite the name of Amitāyus Buddha; thus, in every thought-moment, the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death are eliminated. After life ends, one will immediately attain rebirth. This is taught at length, including what kind of mind is called "the sincere mind" (*zhìxīn*).
What is meant by "the ten moments of mindfulness succeeding one another"?
Master Kumārajīva said:
"It is like a person in a vast wilderness who encounters a band of evil robbers; they brandish spears and draw swords, coming straight at him to kill him."
That person runs with diligence and perceives the crossing of a river; at that time, he thinks only of the means for crossing the river, yet once he has reached the riverbank, he wonders:
"Shall I cross while wearing my clothes, or shall I cross having removed them?"
If I keep my clothes on, I fear I shall not be able to cross;
if I take them off, I fear I shall have no leisure.
To harbor only this thought and no other intention, while keeping in mind the crossing of the river—this alone constitutes a single moment of focused attention.
These ten recitations are not interspersed with other thoughts; the practitioner is likewise so.

Whether reciting the Buddha’s name or contemplating the Buddha’s marks, one recollects the Buddha without interruption for as long as ten recitations. To practice with such single-minded devotion is called "the ten recitations."
This is the ten-fold aspect of the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*).

Although these two fascicles also speak of the ten recitations (*daśa-smṛti*), they likewise contain both the implicit (*neyārtha*) and explicit meanings; however, among them, the explicit ten recitations differ slightly from the intent of the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*.
In that *Contemplation Sūtra*, the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are not excluded, except for the sin of slandering the Vaipulya sūtras;

whereas in these two fascicles of the present sūtra, both the five heinous crimes and the slandering of the True Dharma are excluded. Since these two accounts appear contradictory, how can they be reconciled?
That sutra speaks of those who, although they have committed the five heinous crimes, attain repentance by relying on the Mahayana teachings;
this sutra speaks of those who do not repent. For this reason, there is no contradiction between them.

Some may say: "The 'ten recitations' mentioned in the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* are not spoken regarding the Pure Land alone; they are likewise taught in the fourth section of the *Amitābha-sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra* (the *Guanjing*) with reference to the Pure Land."

The reason for this is that while the ten recollections (daśa-smṛti) spoken of are said not to be the recollections of ordinary beings, they are actually the cultivation of the bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) and the three levels of worthiness (traya-ārya), taking such things as the mind of compassion (maitrī-citta) as their ten recollections.
Therefore, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Superior Aspiration" (*Adhyāśayasaṃcodana-parivarta*), states:
"At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"

As the Buddha has taught regarding the merits and benefits of Amitābha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss, if there are sentient beings who give rise to ten kinds of resolve, and with each and every resolve focus their mindfulness exclusively upon Amitābha Buddha, such persons, at the end of their lives, shall attain rebirth in that Buddha’s world.
“World-Honored One!
What are the ten kinds of minds that must be aroused, by virtue of which one shall attain rebirth in that Buddha-world?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
“Maitreya! These ten kinds of mind cannot be generated by ordinary, foolish people, unwholesome men, or those possessed of afflictions.
What are the ten?
First, to give rise to great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and to have no mind of harm;
second, to give rise to great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and to have no mind of oppression or affliction;
third, to not begrudge one's own body or life for the sake of the Buddha’s true Dharma, but to delight in protecting it.
Fourth, to give rise to supreme patience toward all phenomena and to possess a mind free from attachment;
fifth, not to crave gain, offerings, honor, or respect, but to maintain a mind of pure intention;
sixth, to seek the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes and to never, at any time, have a forgetful mind.
Seventh, to respect and honor all sentient beings without a sense of inferiority;
eighth, to not cling to worldly discourse and to give rise to a mind of certainty regarding the factors of enlightenment;
ninth, to plant various roots of goodness with a pure mind free from defilement.
Tenth, one should give rise to a mind of recollection toward all Tathāgatas, having abandoned all signs.
Maitreya, these are called the ten kinds of minds that a bodhisattva generates; by virtue of these minds, one shall attain rebirth in the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
Maitreya!
If a person, among these ten kinds of mind, achieves even one of them and desires to be reborn in that Buddha-world, it is impossible that they should not be reborn there.
The commentary explains:
This sutra is a different translation of the same original text as the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā*.
Regarding the statement that it cannot be produced by ordinary fools, unwholesome persons, or those possessed of afflictions: "ordinary" refers to those of no spiritual nature (*icchantika*).
The "fools" are those of the two vehicles who seek quiescence;
those who slander the true Dharma and commit the five heinous crimes are called "unwholesome persons possessed of afflictions.
Apart from these, all other people can achieve single-mindedness and attain birth in that land; such a thing is certainly possible.

Therefore, one should understand that when it is said that the "ten recollections" (*daśa-smṛti*) taught by Maitreya are not the recollections of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), this does not mean they are exclusively those cultivated on the stages (*bhūmi*).
If it were otherwise, why would bodhisattvas prior to the stages lack compassion? Would they not go [to the Pure Land] as well?

If one practices the sixteen contemplations as described in the *Contemplation Sūtra* with the aim of being born in that land, the nine grades of practice are explained therein in detail; these shall be discussed in the following section.
If one follows the *Treatise on Rebirth*, it clarifies five causal practices.
As that treatise states:
"If a son or daughter of good family accomplishes the practice of the five gates of mindfulness, they will ultimately attain birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss and behold that Amitābha Buddha."
What are the five gates of mindfulness?
First, the gate of prostration;
second, the gate of praise; [and so forth].
Third, the gate of making vows;
fourth, the gate of observation;
fifth, the gate of dedication.
What is prostration?
It is the physical act of prostrating before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha for the sake of being born in that land.
What is praise?

One praises through the karma of speech, invoking the name of that Tathāgata, in accordance with that Tathāgata’s marks of light and wisdom, and in accordance with the meaning of that name, desiring to practice in accord with reality.
How does one make this vow?
One constantly aspires with a single-minded focus, vowing to be ultimately reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, desiring to practice *śamatha* according to reality.
How does one observe?

One observes with wisdom and contemplates with right mindfulness; because one desires to practice vipaśyanā as it truly is, one first observes the merits of the Buddha-field, and second, observes the merits of the Buddha.
Third, contemplating the merit of the bodhisattva’s adornments.
How does one dedicate [merit]?

By not abandoning sentient beings who suffer all forms of affliction, constantly making vows with the mind, and taking dedication as the foremost priority, thereby achieving the perfection of the great compassionate heart.
The detailed exposition is as described therein;
the causes and conditions for rebirth have been briefly explained in this manner.
Fifth, regarding the enumeration of the chapters on rebirth:
Only the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* speaks of rebirth in that land as being categorized into no more than nine grades; thus, that sūtra says:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively explain for me the place free from sorrow and affliction, so that I may attain rebirth there!"
I take no pleasure in this turbid and evil world of Jambudvīpa.

In this place of defilement and wickedness, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals abound, and there is a great accumulation of unwholesome things. I vow that in the future, I shall not hear evil sounds nor see evil people.

"Now, prostrating myself before the World-Honored One with my five limbs touching the ground, I beg for compassion and repentance; I only pray that the Buddha-Sun will teach me how to contemplate the sphere of pure karma.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from between his eyebrows; the light was golden in color and shone throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, then returned to rest upon the crown of the Buddha's head, transforming into a golden terrace as vast as Mount Sumeru, within which the pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions were all manifested.

There are some lands composed of the seven treasures; furthermore, there are lands consisting entirely of lotus flowers; again, there are lands like the palaces of the god Īśvara; and there are lands like crystal mirrors, wherein the lands of the ten directions all appear. Such immeasurable Buddha-lands, magnificent and clearly visible, were made for Vaidehī to behold.
Then Vaidehī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Although these various buddha-lands are pure and all possess radiance, I now desire to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss, in the presence of Amitābha Buddha.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will teach me how to contemplate and teach me right concentration.
The Buddha said to Vaidehī:
"Do you know now?
Amitābha Buddha is not far from here. You should fix your mindfulness and clearly contemplate that land, where those who have perfected pure karma dwell."
I shall now explain many parables for you, so that all ordinary people in future ages who wish to cultivate pure karma may be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Those who wish to be born in that land must: first, refrain from killing and cultivate the ten wholesome deeds;
second, receive and uphold the Three Refuges, fulfill all the precepts, and not violate the rules of dignified conduct;
third, resolve to attain Bodhicitta, have deep faith in cause and effect, read and recite Mahayana sutras, and encourage others to practice.
"These three matters are called pure karma.
The Buddha told Vaidehī:
"Do you now understand?"
"These three types of karma are the true causes for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the three periods of time.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī:

"Regarding those of the highest grade in the highest birth: if there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land, provided they give rise to three kinds of mind, they shall immediately attain rebirth there."
What are the three?
First, the sincere mind; second, the profound mind;
and third, the mind of dedication.
Third is the mind of dedication and aspiration.
One who possesses these three minds will certainly be born in that land.
Furthermore, there are three types of sentient beings who shall attain rebirth there.
What are these three?
First, to refrain from killing with a mind of loving-kindness and to fulfill all precepts and practices;
second, to read and recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
Third, by practicing the six mindfulnesses, dedicating the merit, and making a vow to be born in that land,
one who possesses these merits will attain rebirth in that very life, after one day up to seven days.
"At the time of being born in that land, because this person has practiced with such diligence and valor,
Amitābha Tathāgata, together with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus,
a great assembly of śrāvakas, immeasurable devas, palaces made of the seven treasures, and the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara..."
Holding the vajra-pedestal, together with the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, they arrive before the practitioner.
Amitābha Buddha emits a great radiance that illuminates the practitioner’s body, and together with the various bodhisattvas, he extends his hands to welcome them.
Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and countless other bodhisattvas praise the practitioner and encourage their resolve.
Upon seeing this, the practitioner rejoices and leaps for joy; beholding himself mounted upon a vajra pedestal, following behind the Buddha, he is reborn in that land in the mere twinkling of an eye.

Having been born in that land, one beholds the Buddha’s physical body, complete with all its marks; one beholds the bodhisattvas, complete with their physical marks; and hears the sublime Dharma being expounded from the radiance and jewel groves. Upon hearing it, one immediately realizes the supreme patience regarding dharmas (*anuttara-dharma-kṣānti*). In the mere interval of a moment, one serves various Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

In the presence of all the Buddhas, they receive successive predictions of enlightenment; returning to their own lands, they attain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharani-doors—these are called those who are born in the highest grade of the highest level.

“Those of the highest grade of middle birth do not necessarily uphold, recite, or chant the Vaipulya sutras; yet they skillfully understand their meaning and intent, their minds are not startled or shaken by the ultimate truth (paramārtha), they have deep faith in cause and effect, and they do not slander the Mahāyāna. By means of these merits, they dedicate them toward the vow to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

When the life of one who practices this path is about to end, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a vast assembly of followers including Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, will arrive before the practitioner holding a purple-golden platform and say:
"O Son of the Dharma!..."
"You practice the Mahāyāna and understand the ultimate truth; therefore, I have now come to welcome you.
At that moment, a thousand transformation Buddhas simultaneously extended their hands.

The practitioner saw himself seated upon a purple-gold pedestal, joining his palms and reverently praising the Buddhas. In the space of a single thought-moment, he was reborn in that land within a pond of the seven treasures.

This purple-golden terrace is like a great jewel flower; it opens after one night has passed. The practitioner’s body becomes the color of purple-polished gold, and beneath his feet there are also lotus flowers made of the seven jewels. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas simultaneously emit radiance that illuminates the practitioner’s body, and his eyes immediately open and become clear. Due to his prior habitual practice, he universally hears various sounds, all of which exclusively expound the profound ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). He then descends from the golden terrace, prostrates before the Buddha with palms joined, and praises the World-Honored One.

After seven days, they immediately attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi; at that same time, they are able to fly to the ten directions to serve various Buddhas in succession, and in the presence of those Buddhas, they cultivate various samādhis. After the passage of one small kalpa, they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and receive a manifest prediction of enlightenment; these are called those of the highest grade of middle birth.

"Regarding those who are born in the lower grade of the highest level: they also believe in cause and effect and do not slander the Mahāyāna; they merely give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and, by means of these merits, dedicate them toward the vow to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss."

When the practitioner’s life is about to end, Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and their retinues, will hold golden lotus flowers and manifest as five hundred Buddhas to come and welcome this person.
Five hundred manifested Buddhas simultaneously extended their hands and praised him, saying:
"Son of the Dharma!
You are now pure; having resolved to attain the unsurpassed Way, we have come to welcome you."

When one sees this, one immediately perceives oneself sitting upon a golden lotus flower; once seated, the flower closes, and following behind the World-Honored One, one attains rebirth within a pond of the seven treasures.
In one day and one night, the lotus flower finally opens;
within seven days, one is able to see the Buddha.
Although one sees the Buddha’s body, the mind does not clearly comprehend the excellence of his various marks.

After twenty-one days, he will see clearly and hear the sounds of various musical instruments all expounding the wondrous Dharma; he will travel throughout the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas, and in the presence of those Buddhas, he will hear the most profound teachings. After three minor kalpas, he will attain the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas and dwell on the Stage of Joy; this is called one who is born in the lower grade of the highest level.
This is called the sign of birth for the highest grade, and is named the Fourteenth Meditation.

"Regarding those born in the middle grade, superior class: if there are sentient beings who observe the eightfold precepts and fasts, practice various moral precepts, do not commit the five heinous crimes, and are free from all faults and afflictions, they take these roots of goodness and dedicate them with the vow to seek rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss."

At the time of death, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a retinue of bhikṣus, will emit golden light and arrive at the person’s side; he will expound upon suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and praise the life of renunciation, whereby one may be freed from all sufferings.

Having seen this, the practitioner’s heart was filled with great joy; he saw himself sitting upon a lotus pedestal, kneeling upright with palms joined, prostrating before the Buddha. Before his head had even been raised, he immediately attained rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and the lotus flower opened at once.

When the flowers bloom, they hear various sounds praising the Four Noble Truths; at that very moment, they immediately attain the path of Arhatship, possessing the three insights, the six supernatural powers, and the eight liberations—these are called those who are reborn in the middle grade of the superior level.
"Regarding those born in the middle grade of the middle level: if there are sentient beings who, for one day and one night, observe the eight precepts of the fast;
or for one day and one night, maintain the śrāmaṇera precepts;

or for one day and one night, maintain the full precepts (upasaṃpad) with unimpaired dignified conduct, and by virtue of this merit, dedicate it toward the vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, perfuming their cultivation with the fragrance of the precepts."

For one who practices in this manner, at the time of death, they will see Amitābha Buddha together with his retinue, emitting golden light and holding a lotus flower made of the seven treasures, appearing before the practitioner.
The practitioner sees a voice in the sky praising him, saying:
"O good son! Since you, a virtuous person, have followed the teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, I have come to welcome you."
The practitioner sees himself seated upon a lotus flower; the lotus then closes, and he is reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Within the precious ground, after seven days have passed, the lotus flower finally unfolds.
Once the flowers had fully blossomed, he opened his eyes, joined his palms, and praised the World-Honored One; hearing the Dharma, he rejoiced and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
After half an eon had passed, he became an Arhat; this is called one who is born in the middle grade within the middle class.
“Regarding those born in the lower grade of the middle level: if there are good men or good women who filially support their parents and practice worldly benevolence and kindness;

when such a person’s life is about to end, they encounter a virtuous friend who extensively explains for them the joyful matters of Amitābha Buddha’s land and also expounds the forty-eight great vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.
Having heard this matter, they immediately pass away; like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, they are reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

Seven days after their birth there, they encounter Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, hear the Dharma with joy, and after the passing of a minor kalpa, they become arhats. These are called those who are born in the lower grade of the middle class.

"Regarding those who are reborn in the highest grade of the lower level: there may be sentient beings who have committed various evil deeds; although they do not slander the Vaipulya sutras, such foolish people have committed many evils and lack a sense of shame or remorse."

When their life is about to end, they encounter a virtuous friend who praises the titles of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras; by hearing the names of these various sūtras, they eliminate the most grievous evil karma accumulated over a thousand kalpas.

The wise one further instructs them to join their palms and press their hands together, reciting "Namo Amitābha Buddha. By reciting the name of the Buddha, they eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over fifty billion kalpas.
At that time, that Buddha immediately dispatched a manifested Buddha, a manifested Avalokiteśvara, and a manifested Mahāsthāmaprāpta to the practitioner’s presence, praising him, saying: “Good son!
"Because you have recited my name, all your transgressions shall be extinguished, and I will come to welcome you.
Having spoken these words, the practitioner immediately beheld the radiance of the transformed Buddha, which filled his entire room.
Having seen this, they rejoice and immediately pass away. Riding upon a precious lotus flower, they follow behind the manifested Buddha and are born within a precious pond.

After seven times seven days have passed, the lotus flower finally blooms. At the moment it blooms, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion emits a great radiance and stands before that person, preaching the profound twelvefold scriptures for them. Having heard this, they believe and understand, giving rise to the mind of supreme enlightenment. After ten minor kalpas, they become fully endowed with the "Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas" and attain entry into the First Stage (Prathamabhūmi). This is called one who is born in the Upper Grade of the Lower Class.
"Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, the name of the Dharma, and the name of the Sangha—having heard the names of the Triple Gem—one immediately attains rebirth there.
'As for those of the middle grade of the lower class: there may be sentient beings who have violated the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the full set of monastic precepts.'"
