Such foolish people steal the property of the Saṃgha at large and pilfer the goods of the present Saṃgha; they preach the Dharma impurely, lacking any sense of shame or remorse, adorning themselves with various evil karmas.
Such a sinner, due to their evil karma, would otherwise fall into hell; yet at the moment their life is about to end, the various fires of hell all arrive simultaneously.

They then encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who, out of great compassion, explains for them the ten powers and majestic virtues of Amitābha Buddha, extensively describing that Buddha’s radiance and supernatural power, and also praising his morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*).

Upon hearing this, that person eliminates the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas; the fierce fires of hell transform into a cool, refreshing breeze that blows celestial flowers, upon each of which there are transformed Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming to welcome them. In a single thought-moment, they immediately attain rebirth within a lotus flower inside a pond of the seven treasures.
After six kalpas had passed, the lotus flower finally blossomed; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta then comforted that person with Brahma-sounds and expounded for them the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.
Having heard this Dharma, they immediately give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment at that very moment.
This is called "the middle birth of the lower grade.

"As for those who attain the lower birth of the lower grade: there may be sentient beings who commit unwholesome deeds, including the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts, being fully possessed of all manner of unwholesomeness. Such foolish people, due to their evil karma, ought to fall into the evil realms and pass through many kalpas, undergoing endless suffering.

When such a foolish person approaches the end of life, they may encounter virtuous spiritual friends who offer various forms of consolation, preach the sublime Dharma to them, and instruct them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Yet, being oppressed by suffering, that person is unable to maintain mindfulness of the Buddha. The virtuous friend then says to them:
"If you are unable to practice mindfulness, you should instead recite the name of Amitāyus Buddha!"
Thus, with such sincerity and ensuring that the sound does not cease, one completes ten recitations, invoking "Namo Amitābha Buddha.
By invoking the name of the Buddha, in every single thought-moment, the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death are eliminated.

After the end of life, one will see a golden lotus flower, like a solar disc, appearing before that person; in the space of a single thought-moment, one will immediately attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss.

Within the lotus flower, for the full duration of twelve great kalpas, the flower finally opens; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with voices of great compassion, extensively expound for them the true reality of all dharmas and the methods for eliminating and extinguishing sins. Having heard this, they rejoice and immediately give rise to the bodhicitta at that very moment.
The commentary explains:
Generally, these nine grades are categorized into two schools of interpretation.

The first school interprets these nine grades as all belonging to Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Depending on whether they advance or regress, and whether they perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds, their ascent and descent differ, thereby forming nine distinct grades.

The first three types of persons belong to the stage of the Ten Faiths; those who proceed directly from the beginning without regression have practices that vary in depth and shallowness, thereby forming the three superior grades.

The middle three types of persons regress from the Mahāyāna mind, give rise to the intent of the Hīnayāna, regress from Mahāyāna practice, and cultivate the karma of the Hīnayāna; their practices also vary in depth and shallowness, thereby forming the three middle grades.

The lower three types of persons regress from the Mahāyāna mind and enter the stream of birth and death; they regress from Mahāyāna practice and commit the offenses of birth and death; these offenses vary in gravity and lightness, thereby forming the three lower grades.
The second explanation states: those who resolve to attain great bodhicitta and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva—whose practice varies in depth—accomplish the three superior grades;
those who resolve for bodhicitta but practice the conduct of a śrāvaka—whose practice varies in depth—accomplish the three middle grades;

and those who do not resolve for the minds of either the Great or Small Vehicles, nor practice the conducts of either vehicle, but instead possess only a mind intent on saṃsāra and commit only the offenses of saṃsāra—depending on whether these committed offenses are heavy or light—they accomplish the three inferior grades.
This constitutes the coarse classification of the nine grades.
If discussed in detail, regarding those born in the highest grade of the highest level, they give rise to three kinds of resolve; as the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The stage of generating the resolve through the perfection of faith occurs at the conclusion of the ten stages of faith."

"Those who, upon being born there, immediately attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)" refers to the patience of observing the non-arising through conditions; this is because the *Benye jing* states that the patience of non-arising belongs to the stage of understanding (*jiewei*).

As for those of "middle birth in the superior grade," their position is at the beginning of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), since one kalpa here is equivalent to one day there; thus, attaining the patience of non-arising after a minor kalpa refers to the patience of non-arising that realizes principle, which corresponds to the first bhūmi.

Those of "lower birth in the superior grade" are those prior to the ten stages of faith, specifically those from the point they place their faith in the Triple Gem and receive the Bodhisattva precepts onward.

Because they also believe in cause and effect, do not slander the Mahāyāna, and have merely resolved to attain the unsurpassed path, for seven days they see only the body of the Buddha, yet their minds do not comprehend it. After three weeks, those who see and hear clearly are said to be individuals who have not yet attained the stage of seeing the Tathāgata through the gateway of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness); it is only after three weeks that they enter the stage of the "Ten Understandings" (*daśa-vyākhyāna*), at which point they realize that the vision of the Buddha arises solely from the mind.

Regarding the statement that one dwells on the Stage of Joy for three small kalpas: these small kalpas correspond here to the asaṃkhyeya kalpa; thus, those of middling capacity pass through one small kalpa, while those of inferior capacity pass through three small kalpas.

Regarding those who enter the first bhūmi together: because the bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) differ in having either sharp or dull faculties and in being either diligent or lax in their practice, there is only a difference in duration—long or short—while their meritorious practice remains equal.
In the subsequent sections below, this may be understood by analogy.
Within the middle three grades, the superior grade refers to the stages of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)—namely, Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*);
the middle grade refers to the first three of the skillful means belonging to the stage of liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
The inferior grade refers to ordinary persons who have attained goodness prior to the five cessations (pañca-nivāraṇa-pratipakṣa).

These three grades of persons are all those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life; they are merely divided into three grades based on the duration of their remaining lifespan, which ranges from half an eon down to a short period.

The three lower grades refer, in general, to all ordinary persons who follow evil destinies and commit various heinous acts; though these acts differ in degree as light or heavy, when they encounter conditions and hear the Dharma to extinguish their offenses, they achieve the three grades, with no further distinctions in rank.
If one follows the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, it generally explains three grades.
As that sūtra states:
"The Buddha addressed Ānanda:"
"Any sentient beings who are born in that land shall all abide in the stage of those destined for rightness (samyaktva-niyāma). Why is this?
Because in that Buddha-land, there are no groups of the wrong (mithyātva-niyāma) nor of the undetermined (aniyata-niyāma)."
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all together praise the inconceivable majestic power and meritorious virtues of Amitāyus Buddha.

Any sentient beings who hear his name and rejoice with faith, even for a single thought-moment, and wholeheartedly dedicate their merit toward rebirth in that land, shall immediately attain rebirth there.
“They shall abide in non-retrogression, with the sole exception of those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“In the worlds of the ten directions, among all devas and humans, there are three classes of people who, with a sincere heart, vow to be born in that land:”

As for those of the highest grade, they leave home and renounce desire to become śramaṇas; they resolve their minds on Bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitāyus Buddha, cultivating various meritorious practices with the aspiration to be born in that land.

When these sentient beings approach the end of their lives, Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great assembly, will appear before them; they shall then be reborn in that land by following that Buddha, spontaneously manifesting through transformation within lotuses made of the seven treasures, abiding in non-retrogression, possessing courageous wisdom and sovereign supernormal powers.
Therefore, Ānanda!
Any sentient beings who wish to see Amitāyus Buddha in this very life should resolve their minds upon unexcelled bodhi, cultivate meritorious virtues, and vow to be born in that land.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“As for those of the middle grade—among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions—who with a sincere heart vow to be born in that land, though they cannot become śramaṇas or extensively cultivate meritorious deeds, they should give rise to the unsurpassed mind of bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively keep Amitāyus Buddha in mind. To whatever extent they cultivate goodness, uphold the fasts and precepts, erect stupas and images, provide food and drink to śramaṇas, hang silk banners, light lamps, scatter flowers, and burn incense, they should dedicate these merits, vowing to be born in that land.”

When that person approaches the end of life, Amitāyus Buddha manifests a transformation body, possessing radiance and the marks and signs of excellence exactly like those of a true Buddha; appearing before that person together with a great multitude, the person is immediately reborn in that land following the transformation Buddha, abiding in non-retrogression, with merit and wisdom equal to those of the highest grade.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"As for those of the lowest grade, among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions, if there are those who with a sincere heart desire to be born in that land, even if they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds, they should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi and focus their intent single-mindedly, reciting the name of Amitāyus Buddha even as many as ten times, vowing to be born in his land."

If one hears this profound Dharma and, with joy, faith, and delight, gives rise to no doubt or confusion, and even for a single moment of thought brings that Buddha to mind, then with a heart of utmost sincerity, one vows to be born in that land.
"When this person approaches the end of life, they will see that Buddha in a dream and attain rebirth there; their merit and wisdom will be next only to those of the middle grade.
You should take this to heart!
Reflect upon this!
Within these matters, you must align your mind and rectify your conduct. To state the essentials:

from the noble ones of the Three Vehicles and the three sages prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), through those of the two vehicles who have developed the mind after the seven expedient means (*upāya*)—these being the nominal bodhisattvas—and even those prior to the path of expedient means, including the fourfold assembly of men and women, those without sexual organs or with dual organs, and even the eight classes of beings such as nāgas and ghosts—if they can simply resolve their minds on Bodhicitta, single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, loathe the defiled lands, and rejoice in the Pure Land.
At the time of death, those for whom right mindfulness manifests before them shall all attain rebirth.
If one is courageous and diligent, such that their contemplative practice is clear and their final mind at the moment of death is undisturbed, they shall together attain birth in the upper realms;
even if one maintains ten consecutive recitations of the Buddha's name at the very last moment of life, provided these manifest before them, they shall attain the lower grade of rebirth.
Among these, the rebirth of Bodhisattvas naturally consists of three grades;
the rebirth of those of the Two Vehicles naturally consists of superior, middling, and inferior grades;
and the rebirth of ordinary beings naturally consists of superior, middling, and inferior grades.

Each category has nine grades; however, the sutras cannot provide a detailed differentiation, as they discuss great and small ordinary beings collectively within these nine grades. In reality, there are actually immeasurable distinctions.
Examining the purport of the Forty-eight Vows and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are those who are born through the primary mode,
while noble ones (*ārya*) are those who are born through both modes.
That sūtra states only:
"For all ordinary beings of future ages who are harmed by the thieves of affliction, I shall preach the locus of pure karma.
Thus he exhorted others to be reborn there, without distinction as to whether they were bodhisattvas or not.
Among ordinary beings, those who slander the Mahāyāna do not attain rebirth there because they have severed their roots of goodness;
among those of the Two Vehicles, practitioners of unwholesome dharmas do not attain rebirth there because they do not believe in the pure lands of the ten directions;
and Bodhisattvas who do not wish to be born there likewise do not go, because they possess the mastery of their aspirational vows.

If those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning—whether their karma be evil or not—are all able to attain rebirth there, because within the defiled lands of the triple world, there is no place for them to take birth.
The general meaning regarding the categories of beings born [in the Pure Land] is thus.

Sixth, regarding the ease or difficulty of rebirth, there are two parts: first, clarifying the superiority and inferiority of the two places; second, clarifying the ease and difficulty of rebirth therein.
First, clarifying the superiority and inferiority of the two places: [text follows].
The subsequent discussion concerns the difficulty and ease of rebirth.
As for speaking of superiority and inferiority: when one praises actual virtues in their entirety, who could be deemed inferior?
Therefore, they are all equally Dharma Kings and are alike called Sugatas; their bodies are endowed with omnipotence, and their lands are filled with every excellence.
It is only for the sake of transforming sentient beings that [the Buddha] sometimes dwells in an impure land, where ruins fill the fields;
or he abides in a pure realm, where wondrous jewels abound.
If one were to discuss these locations, there is indeed no lack of distinction between superior and inferior: the Tuṣita Heaven palace, for instance, is established upon the void.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss is established upon the earth, which distinguishes it from the realms of humans and devas.
If one judges that realm according to the laws of this world, then the devas are superior and humans are inferior;
however, if one considers purity and defilement, Tuṣita is a defiled realm while Sukhāvatī is a pure land.
There are fourteen distinctions between this [Tuṣita] and that [Western Pure Land]: namely, the realm of Tuṣita Heaven is narrow and constricted; it is inhabited by both men and women together;

there is still the manifestation of sensual desire; there is also retrogression; the lifespan is four thousand years, yet there is premature death, and the same applies to body size; furthermore, the three types of mental natures arise, so one may fall into hell through an evil mind; the three feelings arise alternately; the six sensory objects cause heedlessness; sons rest on their fathers' laps and daughters on their mothers' laps; only Bodhisattvas serve as the preachers of the Dharma; and some attain the fruits of sainthood while others do not. If one considers the Western Land, these characteristics are the reverse: it is vast and spacious; it is free from the cohabitation of men and women; there is no manifestation of sensual desire; there is no retrogression; the lifespan is immeasurable and there is no premature death, nor is this the case for body size; the three types of mental natures do not arise, so one does not fall into hell through an evil mind;

the three feelings do not arise alternately; the six sensory objects do not cause heedlessness; sons and daughters rest on lotus thrones; Śākyamuni Buddha serves as the preacher of the Dharma; and all attain the fruits of sainthood. If one considers the meaning according to these points, the Western Land is vastly superior.
The latter part of the treatise discusses the ease or difficulty of rebirth.
Some say that rebirth in the Western Land is easy while rebirth in Tuṣita is difficult, and there are seven distinctions between them:
first, rebirth in Sukhāvatī is easy for humans, whereas rebirth in Tuṣita is difficult for devas.
Second, one may be reborn in Sukhāvatī by merely upholding the five precepts, whereas one must fully cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action to go to Tuṣita;
third, one may go to Sukhāvatī even with as few as ten recitations, whereas one must fully practice giving, morality, and meditation to go to Tuṣita;
fourth, rebirth in the West ultimately relies upon the forty-eight great vows of Amitābha Buddha, whereas rebirth in Tuṣita can only rely upon one’s own power.
Fifth, in the Western Quarter there are Bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara who will come to this land to encourage others to go; in Tuṣita, there is no such thing.
Sixth, the sūtras and śāstras of the Western Quarter fully praise and exhort [one to go], whereas in Tuṣita, it is praised and explained in only one sūtra.
Seventh, since ancient times, there have been many great virtuous ones who have directed themselves toward the Western Quarter, while those who have directed themselves toward Tuṣita have been few.
For this reason, rebirth in the West is easy, whereas rebirth in Tuṣita is difficult.
Alternatively, it is said that rebirth in Tuṣita is easy while rebirth in Sukhāvatī is difficult; how is this known?

The knowledge that the celestial palaces of the Tuṣita Heaven are all contained within this [body] is something accepted by both the great and the small; since they are manifested as transformations, one will certainly be reborn there.

According to the *Sūtra on the Rebirth Above*, if the fourfold assembly practices the six perfections according to the Dharma, the eight classes of beings will rejoice and praise upon hearing their names, repent of their evil karma, cultivate the ten practices, and dedicate their vows toward rebirth there—everyone shall attain it.

Regarding the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), if one follows the "intentional meaning of a different time" (*paryāya-abhisandhi*) from the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, it is like saying that if one has the vow to be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss, one will attain rebirth; the intent lies in a different time, just as one might say "for a single coin, one obtains a thousand. Therefore, that sūtra states:
"One is not born there by means of the causes and conditions of minor roots of goodness.
The *Tianqin lun* (Vasubandhu’s Commentary) states:
"Women, those with impaired faculties, and those of the two vehicles' lineage are not born [there]."
The white hair-tuft mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*) of that Buddha is like five Mount Sumerus; how could those of the class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) be able to see such a mark?
There are many such proofs establishing this meaning. Therefore, I pray that I may not be born even once in the Western [Pure Land].
Some say that both of the preceding two explanations do not fully capture the principle; rather, whether rebirth is difficult or easy depends entirely upon causes and conditions.
"Conditions" refers to the great compassion of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which is of one essence with them;
"causes" refers to the vows and practices initiated by the fourfold assembly and the nine grades of practitioners.
Although the compassion of our shared essence knows no partiality toward individuals, the karma of sentient beings remains uneven.

If the causes of such karma have ripened, may they be reborn accordingly; it is not because the realms of humans or devas are difficult to reach, nor because the pure and impure lands present obstacles.
If one lacks the merit of aspiration and practice, they will have no sincerity before them; how could it be that [the Buddha] would easily manifest his birth within the same realm?

Furthermore, he visited them by means of a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya); thus, although more than three hundred million households resided together in the city of Rājagṛha, none had ever heard the name of the Tathāgata.
Within the *naraka* hells, nine billion beings dwell separately; even those in the house of hardship still come to behold the three golden marks.
Thus one knows that the arising of the conduct of sentient beings truly depends on the connection with superior conditions, whether there is loss or non-loss.
Some have a nature that naturally belongs to Amitābha, while others are originally linked to Maitreya; by following their respective affinities, each attains the Way swiftly.
To force oneself where there is no affinity involves much toil and little benefit.
Therefore, the slave-mother of the Elder was transformed by Rāhula;
the three sons of the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception awakened to the Way through the relinquishment of the body.
Thus, when one entrusts the mind to that which is honored, they compete in their diligent pursuit of their task; such a transition is easy, occurring faster than the snap of a finger.
What need is there for the debate over whether [the path] is difficult or easy?

If one’s resolve is firm and free from doubt, then these six matters are easily distinguished and the nine grades are not difficult to cultivate. Though transgressions may be many, they are dissolved like the darkness dispelled by the rising sun; though the realms of rebirth may be obscure and obstructed, one passes through them as freely as a royal seal opens a barrier.

Yet those who are like apprentices carving a boat or practitioners waiting for a rabbit at a stump doubt the sincere words of the tongue-phenomenon that covers the thousandfold world-system, while believing the well-frog’s discourse of a single ignorant mind.
Is this not like mistaking a common "swallow-stone" for a treasure while harboring doubts about a "Sui-pearl"?
How tragic and lamentable!

Question:
"If the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains this with the intention that it refers to a different time, does this not imply a lack of realization regarding that [point]? Answer:
"In that treatise, it is explained that there are cases where there is a distinction of time and cases where there is no distinction of time.
If one merely makes a vow in emptiness, this constitutes a distinction of time;
if one cultivates both practice and vows together, this is not a distinction of time."

If the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu judged the practice of ten recitations to be intended for a different time, why did he compose the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa* (*Wǎngshēng lùn*) to exhort people toward rebirth there?

Furthermore, regarding the purpose for which the *Amitābha-sūtra* (the *Guan jing*) was taught: it was because Vaidehī, having given birth to Ajātaśatru as a rebellious son, became weary of the five turbidities and vowed to be born in Sukhāvatī.

The Buddha then expounded for them the three meritorious actions and the sixteen contemplation gates, encouraging rebirth through non-arising; he even exhorted those who have committed the ten evil deeds or the five heinous crimes to seek rebirth there as well.

Since the host who invited [the Buddha] to the Pure Land resided within the five turbidities and moreover fathered a rebellious son, yet the Buddha declared that both were reborn there, we know for certain that ordinary beings currently dwelling in the five turbidities can all attain rebirth.
Question:
"Vaidehī was a great bodhisattva who, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, manifested in a female body and gave birth to a rebellious son.
How could she truly be of the class of ordinary beings?"

Answer: "Even if one were truly a Bodhisattva manifesting in a female body to transform sentient beings, one must conceal one's actual capabilities and manifest as an ordinary person to gather and transform those of the same kind.
Thus, manifesting as an ordinary person while dwelling in the five turbidities, one always knows how to lead these ordinary beings of the five turbidities to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss."
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"By merely making a vow, it refers to a different time.
Therefore, one should know that the three types of merit, the sixteen contemplations, and the seven-day practice of mindfulness of the Buddha—how could these not also refer to different times?
Question:
"As stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-śāstra*:
'Women and those with impaired faculties, as well as those of the Two Vehicles, are not born [there].'"
"How is it that women and the other three [categories] can also attain rebirth there?
He replied:
"In principle, this is indeed so; if they possess the seeds [of the practice], they will certainly attain rebirth."
Regarding those of "true seed":

first, within this land, there may be men or women whose seed, due to the female cause, is certain to produce female organs; such persons, even if they cultivate practices for the Pure Land, will not attain rebirth there.
Because there are no women in the Pure Land, this is a fixed karma that cannot be altered through exhortation; it is thus an obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).
It should be understood that those with deficient faculties, such as the blind and the deaf, are likewise [subject to fixed karma].
If there is repentance and removal [of offenses], one does not enter among their ranks.
As for those of the Two Vehicles, having planted the seeds of the Two Vehicles, they do not believe in the Mahāyāna or the pure lands of the ten directions; thus, they likewise cannot be born there.
"The 'seeds' elucidated in that treatise refer specifically to the seeds of determinate karma.
Question:
"If this is so, why does the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* state:..."
"By upholding the five precepts, one is immediately reborn there.
Upon hearing the exposition of the Four Noble Truths, one realizes the fruits of the Stream-enterer and so forth. Answer:
"This person who is not deluded regarding the Dharma believes in the Buddhas of the ten directions and their pure lands, and makes a vow to be reborn there.

Once they have realized the fruit of their attainment, the Buddha preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for them, and they turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna; this is the judgment of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*."
Question:
"The evil karma of sentient beings is extremely heavy; it can obstruct rebirth in the Pure Land and cannot be eliminated by minor virtues. Why, then, does the *Contemplation Sūtra* state:
'If one has ten recitations at the moment of death, one will immediately attain rebirth'?"
[Question: "What is it? [Answer:
"The mind is the master of the house; it is the root of rebirth."
The mind at the moment of death is like the eyes, for it can direct all karma.
If the mind at the moment of death is evil, it can lead to all evil karma;
if the mind is virtuous, it can lead to all virtuous karma.
"As the dragon moves, the clouds follow; if the mind departs toward the west, karma follows it as well.
Question: "As stated in the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* regarding the ten recollections (*daśa-smṛti*), it says:"
"It is not the mindfulness of an ordinary person; it is mindfulness unmixed with the fetters and afflictions.
Now, these sentient beings are by nature ordinary persons whose fetters and afflictions have not been severed; how then can they be born [in the Pure Land] through mindfulness of the Buddha?
Answer: "Some say:

'If it were according to that sutra, only the Buddha alone could attain birth, while others would all be unable to do so, because only the Bodhisattva at the final moment of the tenth stage possesses the two kinds of ignorance.'"

Now, to explain that sutra: as for what is called "the mindfulness of ordinary beings," if one does not resolve to attain bodhicitta and seek rebirth beyond the three realms to become a Buddha, but instead merely practices mindfulness of the Buddha with the sole aim of seeking rebirth, this is the mindfulness of an ordinary being; such a person shall not attain birth [in the Pure Land].
Therefore, one must in all cases resolve to attain Bodhicitta.

Regarding "unmixed thoughts free from fetters" (kleśa): one need only maintain a continuous single-mindedness while contemplating the Buddha’s marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana). If, however, one recites the Buddha's name with the mouth while the mind is preoccupied with the five desires, this constitutes "mixed thoughts with fetters."
Mindfulness of the Buddha is a pure mind that is contrary to the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
"Or there may be a different interpretation; see what was stated previously. Question:
"The transgressions and karma of sentient beings are piled up as high as mountains; how could ten recitations possibly extinguish such a vast amount of evil karma?

Even if one were to recite them hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions of times, it would still be too few. If these evil karmas are not extinguished, how else could one attain rebirth in the Pure Land?"
Answer: "There are three meanings:

first, if at the time of death right mindfulness manifests before one, this mind can draw forth all the wholesome karma accumulated from beginningless time as well as that performed throughout one's current life; through their mutual support, one immediately attains rebirth."

Second, the names of the Buddhas are formed by the totality of ten thousand virtues; if one can recite even a single thought of a Buddha’s name, then within that single thought one is reciting all ten thousand virtues. Thus, one extinguishes sinful karma. Since evil karma obstructs progress, once sin is eliminated, what can bind you?
Therefore, it is said in the *Lower Grades of Birth*:
"By invoking the name of the Buddha, the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death are eliminated in every thought-moment.
Third, beginningless evil karma arises from the deluded mind;
The merit of mindfulness of the Buddha arises from the true mind.
The true mind is like the sun, while the deluded mind is like darkness.
When the true mind briefly arises, deluded thoughts are immediately eliminated.
Just as when the sun first rises, all darkness is dispelled;
by virtue of these three meanings, even those who achieve ten recitations at the time of death will certainly attain rebirth.
Question:
"The Pure Land is supreme and wondrous; it is the abode of the Dharma King and the Lotus Treasury, not a place for ordinary beings to practice.

In principle, the ordinary should walk upon the ground of the ordinary, and the sage should tread upon the field of the sage. How could an inferior ordinary being possibly be born in such a wondrous place?"
He replied:
"An ordinary person cannot roam in the Pure Land;
since you are already the Dharma King, how could you tread upon the five turbidities?"
Although he is a Dharma King, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he wanders through the five turbidities;
and although he is an ordinary person, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, he is born in a pure land.

Furthermore, regarding the forty-eight great vows, they were first established for all ordinary beings and subsequently extended to the noble ones of the three vehicles; thus we know that the essential intent of the Pure Land school is fundamentally for ordinary beings, while also encompassing the noble ones.
Furthermore, from the stage of the ten abidings (daśa-vyavakrānti) onward, one does not fear rebirth in the evil realms; therefore, one may aspire to be born in the Pure Land.
Thus we know that the profound intent of the Pure Land is fundamentally for the sake of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), and not for the sake of bodhisattvas.
Question:

"Having personally encountered favorable conditions, I have been reborn into the nine grades of birth and have repeatedly studied the text and its meaning; my mind of indignation has now been dispelled like clouds parting.

Yet, if there are those who committed many evils, did not know how to cultivate goodness, and have already entered the three miserable realms—is there a skillful means to rescue those deceased spirits, to cause them to eliminate their karmic obstructions and be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss?"
Answer: "The sentiments of the ignorant are difficult to penetrate, yet the holy teachings possess skillful means.
Thus, the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Amoghapāśakalparāja-sūtra*, in the chapter titled 'The Accomplishment of the Consecration Mantra,' states:"

"At that time, all Tathāgatas of the three periods throughout all lands in the ten directions, including Vairocana Tathāgata, simultaneously extended their right hands of fearlessness and stroked the crown of the head of the Pure Lotus Radiance King (Vimalaprabhā-rāja).

They spoke in unison this mantra of the Great Infallible Empowerment Light: "Oṃ vairocana mahāmudrāmaṇi padmajvālā parākrama hūṃ. "If there are sentient beings who, wherever they may be, hear this mantra of the Great Empowerment Light two, three, or seven times as it passes through their faculty of hearing, they shall immediately eliminate all karmic obstructions and hindrances."
If all sentient beings were to commit the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, and the four grave offenses, as numerous as motes of dust filling this entire world;

When their bodies perish and their lives end, they would otherwise fall into the various evil realms; however, by consecrating earth and sand one hundred and eight times with this mantra and scattering it over the remains of the deceased in a *śītavana* (cemetery), or scattering it upon their graves—whenever such an occasion arises—the deceased, whether in the hells, among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), among the asuras, or among the animals (*tiryagyoni*), shall, through the power of the original vows of all the Akṣobhya Tathāgatas and the Akṣobhya-Vairocana Tathāgata’s mantra, and by the force of the Great Consecration Light Mantra, immediately obtain radiance and a body, have all karmic retributions for sins eliminated, cast off their suffering bodies, and proceed to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) to be born by transformation within a lotus flower, never again falling back until they reach enlightenment.
"Such scriptural passages appear frequently; how regrettable!
One creates one's own karmic offenses, and the bitter fruits follow like a shadow. How painful!
To suffer alone with solitary calamity, with no one to provide rescue or protection."
Were it not for the Great Compassion that shares the same essence, who could unlock the profound key and ascend to the Flower Bank Terrace through the secret arts of vast salvation?
Although there is no principle of receiving the fruit without another’s action, there exists the inconceivable power of dependent origination.
Thus we know that when one encounters this mantra, there is an immediate affinity; if one does not receive the sand, how can one discuss the timing of liberation?
Only those whose great compassion is boundless and whose long tongue is pure will act and believe; for those who do not act or believe, there shall be no turning back from their subsequent regret.
Thus, those who do not act with sincerity merely carry a heavy debt of gratitude while their repayment grows ever more distant;
whereas those who follow the path of obedience receive their souls upon the lotus of glory, and filial piety and compliance are thereby established.
Fortunately, we have encountered the True Word (Mantra), which makes escape from suffering not difficult; among all gentlemen, who would not practice it?
Even scattering sand upon a grave can lead one to the Pure Land, how much more so when the incantation is worn upon the body and its sounds and characters are heard and recited?
